text: The rules they shaped became the FHA Underwriting Manual.
That manual was not a private opinion.
It was a federal instruction book sent to lenders across the nation.
Read the 1938 edition and the logic is plain.
It tells appraisers to study whether incompatible racial groups are present near a property.
It praises natural or artificial barriers, a river, a wide road, a park, that could keep a neighborhood, in its words, protected from adverse influences.
It openly recommends a deed clause barring the wrong people, and gives that clause extra points.
The prejudice Hoyt charted in 1933 was now a checklist a bank used to say yes or no.
Think about the scale of that.
The FHA would go on to insure tens of billions of dollars in home loans over the following decades, and that wealth built the American middle class one mortgage at a time.
The manual decided who got in line for it.
A white family in a quiet suburb was a safe bet.
A Black family on the South Side was a hazard by definition, whatever their savings or their record.
Between 1945 and 1959, Black Americans received less than two percent of all federally insured home loans.
The subsidy flowed one way, and a generation of equity piled up on one side of the line.
